parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what two quantities a moving object must have for its motion to be hard to stop - how heavy it is and how fast it is moving.
parts.proper_answer: Linear momentum is the product of mass and velocity, $p = mv$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What momentum means**
Think of momentum as the quantity of motion. A heavy slow lorry and a light fast bullet can both be hard to stop. So you need both mass $m$ and velocity $v$ together.

Step 2: **Exact definition**
Momentum is defined by $$p = m \times v$$ It is a vector, so it has direction the same as the velocity, with SI unit $\text{kg m s}^{-1}$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
key_concepts: force as rate of change of momentum
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 2.2 for block Y - when does its momentum first start to change from zero, and when does it stop changing and become flat again?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **When is there a force on Y?**
Block Y is stationary with zero momentum until X touches it. While they touch, X pushes Y so the momentum of Y changes. Once they separate, there is no more push, so the momentum of Y stays constant.

Step 2: **Read the start and end from the graph**
In Fig. 2.2 the graph leaves zero at $t = 60\text{ ms}$ and stops rising at $t = 100\text{ ms}$. So contact lasts $$\Delta t = 100 - 60 = 40\text{ ms}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)1.
hints: Hint 1: From $t = 80\text{ ms}$ to $100\text{ ms}$ the momentum graph is a straight sloping line - what does a constant gradient tell you about the rate of change of momentum and hence the acceleration?
parts.proper_answer: The magnitude of the acceleration is constant (non-zero).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link gradient to acceleration**
Force is rate of change of momentum, $$F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$$ which is the gradient of a $p$-$t$ graph. Since $F = ma$, a constant gradient means constant acceleration.

Step 2: **Apply to 80 to 100 ms**
Between $80\text{ ms}$ and $100\text{ ms}$ the graph is straight with the same steep slope, so $\Delta p / \Delta t$ is constant. The magnitude of acceleration of Y is therefore constant and non-zero.

hints: Hint 1: From $t = 100\text{ ms}$ to $120\text{ ms}$ the momentum of Y is flat - if momentum is not changing, what must the resultant force and acceleration be?
parts.proper_answer: The magnitude of the acceleration is zero.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Flat graph means no change**
From $100\text{ ms}$ to $120\text{ ms}$ the momentum stays at $0.50\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$. So $$\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = 0$$

Step 2: **No force, no acceleration**
Zero rate of change of momentum means zero resultant force on Y, so from $F = ma$ the acceleration magnitude is zero. The blocks have separated and Y moves at constant velocity.

parts.label: (c)
key_concepts: Newton's second law as rate of change of momentum
hints: Hint 1: Force is the rate of change of momentum, so focus on the sloping section where Y gains momentum - what is the total change in momentum and over what time?
Hint 2: Convert the contact time to seconds and divide the momentum change by this time to get force in newtons.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the governing law**
Force on Y equals its rate of gain of momentum: $$F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$$ This is the gradient of the sloping part of Fig. 2.2.

Step 2: **Find change in momentum and time**
Momentum of Y rises from $0$ to $0.50\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$, so $\Delta p = 0.50\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$. Contact time from (b)(i) is $$\Delta t = 40\text{ ms} = 40 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}$$

Step 3: **Calculate the force**
$$F = \frac{0.50}{40 \times 10^{-3}} = 12.5\text{ N} \approx 13\text{ N}$$ This is the magnitude of the force exerted by X on Y during contact.

parts.label: (d)
hints: Hint 1: Before contact X feels no force, so what should its momentum graph look like from $t = 0$ to $t = 60\text{ ms}$ given it starts at $0.40\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$?
Hint 2: Total momentum must stay at $0.40\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ because there are no external forces - if Y ends at $0.50\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$, what must the final momentum of X be?
Hint 3: During contact X loses momentum at the same rate Y gains it, so how should the slope of X between $60\text{ ms}$ and $100\text{ ms}$ compare to the slope of Y?
parts.proper_answer: Horizontal line at $0.40\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ from $t=0$ to $60\text{ ms}$, straight line down to $-0.10\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ at $t=100\text{ ms}$, then horizontal at $-0.10\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ to $160\text{ ms}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Before collision - constant momentum**
From $t = 0$ to $60\text{ ms}$ there is no contact and no friction, so X keeps its initial momentum. Draw a horizontal line from $(0, 0.40)$ to $(60, 0.40)$ in units $\text{kg m s}^{-1}$ and $\text{ms}$.

Step 2: **Use conservation to find the end point**
Total momentum is conserved at $0.40\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$. At the end: $$p_X + p_Y = 0.40$$ With $p_Y = 0.50\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$, $$p_X = 0.40 - 0.50 = -0.10\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$$ The negative sign means X rebounds backwards. So the graph must finish at $-0.10$.

Step 3: **During and after collision**
During contact, $60$ to $100\text{ ms}$, X loses momentum steadily while Y gains it, so draw a straight line from $(60, 0.40)$ down to $(100, -0.10)$. After $100\text{ ms}$ the blocks are separate, so draw a horizontal line from $(100, -0.10)$ to $(160, -0.10)$.
